title: RTO and RPO Planning
description: Learn how to define Recovery Time Objectives and Recovery Point Objectives to choose the right DR strategy.

data.text: **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** and **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** are the two key metrics that define your disaster recovery requirements. Together, they determine which DR strategy fits your business needs.

data.title: Definitions
items: **RTO** — the maximum acceptable downtime before the business suffers serious harm. If your RTO is 1 hour, you must be able to recover within 1 hour of a failure.
**RPO** — the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. If your RPO is 15 minutes, you can lose at most 15 minutes of data.

data.title: RTO and RPO by DR Strategy

cards.title: Pilot Light
cards.description: Core infrastructure running; app scales on demand.

cards.title: Warm Standby
cards.description: Scaled-down environment ready to scale up.

data.text: Business continuity planning (BCP) is the broader process of ensuring critical business functions continue during and after a disruption. DR is just one part of BCP, which also includes incident response, communication plans, and workforce continuity.

data.title: Cost vs Recovery Tradeoffs
items: Lower RTO and RPO require more expensive, redundant infrastructure
Higher RTO and RPO mean cheaper infrastructure but more risk
Balance the cost of downtime against the cost of extra resources

data.title: Planning Advice
data.text: Start by identifying your critical systems and acceptable downtime. Not all systems need the same DR strategy. Tier your applications by importance.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime
RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss
Lower RTO/RPO means higher cost and complexity
Tier your systems by importance to optimize DR spending
